title: Article 254 — Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States

content.overview: Article 254 — Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States. Complete constitutional treatise with procedural anchors, cases, and chamber drafting blueprints.
content.glance: Article 254 — Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States. Complete constitutional treatise with procedural anchors, cases, and chamber drafting blueprints.
content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 254 of the Constitution of India is titled “Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States”. It forms an integral component of Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), located within the “Centre–State” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.

(2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State 1 [omitted with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:

Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 254 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.
2. (2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State 1 [omitted with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:
3. Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 254 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 254 (Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 254 (Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 254 is situated in Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), governing the “Centre–State” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.
2. (2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State 1 [omitted with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:
3. Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 254:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 254 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 254 of the Constitution of India, titled “Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within Relations between the Union and the States (Articles 245–263), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 254 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) If any provision of a law made by the Legislature of a State is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament which Parliament is competent to enact, or to any provision of an existing law with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List, then, subject to the provisions of clause (2), the law made by Parliament, whether passed before or after the law made by the Legislature of such State, or, as the case may be, the existing law, shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void.
(a) Limb 2: (2) Where a law made by the Legislature of a State 1 [omitted with respect to one of the matters enumerated in the Concurrent List contains any provision repugnant to the provisions of an earlier law made by Parliament or an existing law with respect to that matter, then, the law so made by the Legislature of such State shall, if it has been reserved for the consideration of the President and has received his assent, prevail in that State:
(a) Limb 3: Provided that nothing in this clause shall prevent Parliament from enacting at any time any law with respect to the same matter including a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing the law so made by the Legislature of the State.
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 254 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 254 across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 254:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 254;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 254 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 254?
Rule: Under Article 254, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 254 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 254 resolves conflicts (repugnancy) between laws made by Parliament and laws made by State Legislatures with respect to matters enumerated in the Concurrent List (List III). Under Clause (1), if a State law is repugnant to a Central law, the Central law prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy. However, under Clause (2), if a State law on a Concurrent subject has been reserved for and received the assent of the President, it prevails in that State, subject to Parliament's overriding proviso enabling subsequent legislation.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: In the Concurrent field where both sovereigns possess legislative competence, national uniformity yields to localized state requirements ONLY when the President explicitly assents to the State's departure from Central law. Even then, Parliament retains ultimate legislative sovereignty to re-occupy the field and override the State law by subsequent enactment.
statutoryFramework: Part XI: Relations Between the Union and the States, Chapter I: Legislative Relations
Article 254 of the Constitution of India (Clauses 1 and 2, and Proviso)
Interplay with Article 200 and Article 201 (Reservation of Bills for Presidential Assent)
Governed by Constitution Bench precedents: Zaverbhai (1954), Tika Ramji (1956), Deep Chand (1959), and M. Karunanidhi (1979)
essentialIngredients: Concurrent Field Requirement: Repugnancy under Article 254 arises strictly when both the Central law and the State law are enacted with respect to a matter in the **Concurrent List (List III)** (Deep Chand; Hoechst Pharmaceuticals).

Three Tests of Repugnancy (M. Karunanidhi): (1) Direct conflict between two provisions where compliance with one involves disobedience of the other; (2) Operational incompatibility; (3) Occupied field — Parliament intended to lay down an exhaustive, complete code on the subject-matter.
Consequence of Conflict (Clause 1): The Parliamentary enactment prevails, whether passed before or after the State law, and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy.

Presidential Assent Exception (Clause 2): A State law repugnant to an earlier Central law prevails in that State IF: (a) It was reserved for the consideration of the President; AND (b) Has received the assent of the President.
Parliamentary Overriding Proviso: Parliament may at any time enact subsequent legislation adding to, amending, varying, or repealing the State law so preserved under Clause (2).
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 254 is the constitutional referee governing the shared Concurrent List.

### 1. The Definitive Tests of Repugnancy
In *M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India (1979)*, a 5-judge Constitution Bench formulated the authoritative propositions on repugnancy:
1. There must be a clear and direct inconsistency between the Central Act and the State Act.
2. The inconsistency must be of such a nature that the two acts cannot stand together or be reconciled (obedience to one involves disobeying the other).
3. If the Central Act occupies the entire field and exhibits an intention to be an exhaustive code, a State Act entering the same field is repugnant even if it does not directly contradict the Central text.
4. Where two enactments operate in different fields without collision, there is no repugnancy.

### 2. The Presidential Assent Exception (Article 254(2))
Clause (2) embodies asymmetric cooperative federalism:
- A State can enact a law departing from an existing Central Act on a Concurrent matter (e.g., land acquisition amendments, consumer protection rules).
- If the Governor reserves the Bill under Article 200 and the President grants assent under Article 201, the State law **prevails in that State** over the prior Central law.
- **Kaiser-I-Hind Pvt. Ltd. v. National Textile Corp. (2002):** A Constitution Bench held that for Article 254(2) to operate, the State Government must have explicitly pointed out the specific Central law and the exact repugnancy to the President when seeking assent; a vague, general assent does not cure repugnancy.

### 3. The Proviso: Ultimate Parliamentary Overrule
Even after a State law receives Presidential assent under Clause (2), the federal balance tilts back to the Union: Parliament can at any time enact a fresh statute with respect to the same matter, directly adding to, amending, or overriding the State law (*Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay, 1954*).
examples: Presidential Assent Curing Repugnancy: Parliament enacts a central land acquisition statute. A State Legislature enacts an amendment modifying the compensation formula and land return timelines for that State. The Bill is reserved for and receives the assent of the President under Article 254(2). The State amendment validly prevails within that State over the Central statute.

Subsequent Parliamentary Overrule: A State labor law amendment was granted Presidential assent under Article 254(2) in 2020. In 2025, Parliament passes the comprehensive Industrial Relations Code covering the identical field and explicitly covering all establishments nationwide. Under the Proviso to Article 254(2), the subsequent Parliamentary Code overrides the State amendment.
distinctions: Article 254 Repugnancy vs Article 246 Ultra Vires: Ultra vires under Article 246 arises when a legislature lacks competency (e.g., State enacting on List I); Repugnancy under Article 254 arises when both legislatures are fully competent on List III, but their enactments conflict.

Article 254(1) General Rule vs Article 254(2) Exception: Clause (1) establishes Union supremacy over State laws; Clause (2) creates an exception allowing State law to prevail locally if it receives Presidential assent.
problemApplication: Issue: Parliament enacts the Central Motor Vehicles Act under List III Entry 35, setting a maximum speeding fine of Rs. 2,000. A State Legislature passes an amendment raising the fine to Rs. 10,000 within the State. The Governor assents to the State Bill without reserving it for the President. Is the State amendment valid?

Rule: Under Article 254(1), where a State law on a Concurrent subject is repugnant to a Parliamentary law, the Parliamentary law prevails and the State law is void unless saved by Presidential assent under Article 254(2).

Application: Both laws operate in the Concurrent List on the identical subject (penalties for speeding). The state penalty conflicts with the Central scheme. Because the Governor did not reserve the Bill for the President, Article 254(2) is not triggered.
Counterargument: The State argues that traffic regulation is an urgent local safety concern within state police powers.
Conclusion: In the absence of Presidential assent under Article 254(2), the State amendment is void for repugnancy under Article 254(1); the Central Act prevails.

keyTakeaways: Applies strictly to conflicts between Central and State laws on the Concurrent List (List III).
Under Clause (1), Central law prevails and State law is void to the extent of repugnancy.
Under Clause (2), State law prevails in that State if reserved for and assented to by the President (Kaiser-I-Hind).
Parliament can override the assented State law at any time by subsequent enactment under the Proviso.
Three tests of repugnancy: Direct conflict, operational incompatibility, and occupied field (M. Karunanidhi).
